topic.title: the shagun diary
topic.claim: Every Indian family keeps a shagun diary: wedding envelopes are open accounts, and the extra ₹1 keeps them open.

cover.headline: Every Indian family keeps an account book nobody admits exists.

paragraphs: Every Indian family keeps an account book nobody admits exists.
It's the shagun diary.
After every wedding, someone sits down with the envelopes and a notebook. Name, amount, relation.
Nobody calls it accounting. It's exactly that.
Because the envelope isn't really a gift. It's a loan with no paperwork.
When Sharma ji's daughter gets married, someone will open that notebook to check what he gave.
And you never return the same amount. ₹2,100 comes back as ₹3,100.
Returning it exactly would settle the account. Adding a little keeps it open.
That's what the extra ₹1 is doing too. Not ₹500, but ₹501.
A round number ends in zero, and zero is an ending. The rupee says this continues.
So here's the actual rule. In the West, a wedding gift closes the deal: the couple lists a registry, you buy the toaster, everyone's even.
An Indian gift is built never to close.
Do the maths on one wedding. 400 guests at an average of ₹1,100, and the family goes home with ₹4.4 lakh.
And 400 open accounts.
There's a second layer. The diary doesn't only track money; it tracks who came.
The cousin who sent ₹501 on GPay and skipped the wedding is remembered longer than the one who came with ₹101.
So when your parents insist you attend the wedding of people you've met twice, they're not being social.
They're paying an instalment on an account opened before you were born.
Indian families don't lose touch. They just carry a balance.
The ₹1 makes sure it never hits zero.
